routes.description: Traditional authorship is supported by early attribution testimony considered alongside internal features connecting the texts to the named apostles or their associates.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the external traditions and internal textual features jointly make responsibility by Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John more probable than late anonymous attribution.

motionBridge.description: The convergent historical evidence makes traditional responsibility for the canonical Gospels the most reasonable account.

centralBridges.description: Early, geographically distributed, substantially unanimous testimony preserves genuine information about Gospel authorship.
Internal narrative and source features fit the traditionally identified authors or authoritative eyewitness sources.
The objections from anonymity and delayed attribution do not defeat authorship when comparable ancient attribution practices are applied consistently.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The relatively less prestigious names Mark and Luke are improbable choices for an authority-enhancing fabrication.
Collaboration or educated assistance could connect a traditional source with a polished Greek literary product.

routes.description: Anonymous circulation, late naming, educational mismatch, and alternative diffusion explanations undermine identification of the canonical texts with the traditional figures.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the evidence does not reliably connect the surviving Greek texts to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John and is better explained by later attribution.

motionBridge.description: The canonical Gospels should not be attributed directly or authoritatively to the four traditional figures on the evidence presented.

centralBridges.description: Unambiguous identification of the surviving four texts occurs too late to establish continuous authorial knowledge.
The traditional apostolic figures lack the demonstrated Greek literary education required to compose the canonical narratives.
Later unanimity can arise through dependence on a common naming tradition rather than independent historical memory.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Internal features such as detailed narration or occupational vocabulary do not identify the traditional authors.
The proposed amanuensis mechanism lacks a demonstrated ancient parallel for composing extended literary narratives.

sections.title: Early testimony and anonymous circulation
sections.rationale: This section contains the principal affirmative external-evidence case and the negative's earliest comprehensive challenge concerning anonymity, identification, and the date of secure attribution.

sections.title: Internal evidence, literacy, and Johannine authorship
sections.rationale: This section tests the strongest internal identification claims for Luke and John against the demographic literacy objection and the Fourth Gospel's distinction between witness and authorial voice.

sections.title: Ancient parallels, Papias, and collaborative composition
sections.rationale: This section captures the strongest direct rebuttal exchange over anonymity, comparative ancient attribution, Papias, Justin, and the proposed mechanism of literate assistance.

sections.title: Why the traditional names were chosen
sections.rationale: This compact exchange tests a decisive explanatory prediction of the late-naming hypothesis: whether Mark and Luke are implausibly weak fabricated names or strategically useful apostolic associates.

sections.title: Competing explanations of later unanimity
sections.rationale: The closing exchange integrates the external and internal cases and directly tests whether geographic unanimity reflects independent early memory or diffusion from a common late-second-century source.
